questions.q: Why shouldn't the frontend store pool reserves as its own persistent, trusted copy?
options: Reserves change with every swap anyone makes, so a cached copy can silently drift out of sync with the chain
Storing numbers in React state is technically impossible
wagmi forbids storing any contract data locally
Reserves never change once a pool is deployed
questions.explain: Because any user's swap changes reserveA and reserveB, a frontend that caches those values and trusts the cache will show stale, potentially very wrong numbers — the contract must stay the source of truth.

questions.q: Which wagmi hook is used to call a contract's view function and keep the result current, as shown in this lesson?
options: useWriteContract
useReadContract
useSwapQuote
useAccount
questions.explain: useReadContract (built on viem) is the hook this lesson uses to call view functions like reserveA and reserveB and track their current value.

questions.q: What does the useSwapQuote function shown in this lesson compute?
options: A client-side preview of swap output that mirrors the contract's own constant-product formula and fee exactly
The gas price for the next block
The user's total portfolio value across all tokens
A random estimate unrelated to the contract's actual math
questions.explain: useSwapQuote applies the same 0.3% fee and constant-product formula as SimplePool.swapAforB, purely off-chain, so the preview shown to the user matches what the contract will actually compute.

questions.q: Why does swapping an ERC-20 token typically require two separate transactions in this frontend's flow?
options: Because wagmi is slow and splits every call into two steps
Because an ERC-20 token requires an explicit approve call before another contract can move it via transferFrom
Because Sepolia requires double-signing for all transactions
There's no real reason; it's an arbitrary UI choice
questions.explain: ERC-20 tokens require the owner to call approve(spender, amount) before the spender contract (the pool, via transferFrom) can move those tokens, which is why the UI needs a separate approve step before the swap.

questions.q: What does useWriteContract do, per this lesson?
options: Sends a state-changing transaction through the connected wallet and tracks its pending/success/error status
Only reads data without ever requiring a wallet signature
Deletes a deployed contract from the blockchain
Compiles Solidity source code in the browser
questions.explain: useWriteContract is the wagmi hook used to send state-changing calls like swapAforB through the user's connected wallet, with the wallet prompting a signature and the hook exposing transaction status.
